content.title: About
content.content: Pancakes are thin, round flatbreads made from a liquid batter cooked on a skillet. Traditionally they are prepared with wheat flour, eggs, milk, and a small amount of sugar. Pancakes can be served sweet or savory, often topped or filled with a variety of ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pancakes are known worldwide under different names: French crêpes, Russian blini, Ethiopian injera.
In Russia, pancakes are a central part of Maslenitsa, a festival marking the end of winter.
The largest pancake ever made was over 15 meters in diameter, cooked in the United States in 2012.
Pancake contests often feature creative fillings such as seafood, chocolate, or exotic fruits.
There are more than 30 batter variations, including buckwheat, oat, and gluten‑free versions.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pancakes provide quick‑release energy thanks to the carbohydrates in the batter.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk add a modest amount of complete protein to the dish.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and milk supply B1, B2, and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pancakes provide calcium, iron, and magnesium, beneficial for bones and nerves.

items.title: Dietary flexibility
items.content: The recipe can be adapted with whole‑grain flour, plant‑based milk, or egg substitutes to meet various dietary needs.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional wheat‑flour pancakes may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Pancakes can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which is important for individuals with diabetes to monitor.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Cooking with oil can increase the fat content; using a small amount of oil or a non‑stick pan reduces this.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Some ready‑mix pancake mixes contain preservatives and additives that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pancakes hot, rolled or folded. They can be brushed with butter, drizzled with honey, jam, or sour cream, and filled with meat, fish, cheese, vegetables, or fruit. For a lighter option, use whole‑grain or gluten‑free flour.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. They can also be frozen in a stack separated by parchment paper and reheated in a microwave or skillet.

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato (NFS) is a whole tuber baked in its skin without added fats. It retains most of its nutrients, has a characteristic aroma and a tender interior. The product is commonly used as a side dish or a standalone meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baked potatoes retain up to 80 % of vitamin C, which is lost during boiling.
The skin provides dietary fiber that supports digestion.
In the United States, baked potatoes are often served with sour cream, cheese, or chives.
Potatoes are one of the most consumed vegetables worldwide, with over 350 million tonnes produced annually.
Baking at 200 °C creates a crisp crust rich in antioxidants.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Baked potato contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Green spots and sprouts contain solanine, a toxin that should be removed before cooking.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Baked potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly; individuals with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked potato can be eaten hot, split open and topped with butter, sour cream, cheese, herbs or spices. It is also used in salads, casseroles, and as a base for various fillings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked baked potatoes in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to restore a crisp skin.

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka and water is a ready‑to‑drink blend containing 40% vodka and 60% clean drinking water. It is commonly used in bars and restaurants for quick preparation of light cocktails or as a base for diluting strong spirits.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend allows precise control of drink strength without measuring separate ingredients.
It is often served in chilled glasses, enhancing the feeling of freshness.
In some countries the mixture is sold in concentrated sachets that are reconstituted with water just before serving.
The blend can be used in cooking, for example to marinate fish or to make sauces.

items.title: Moderated alcohol intake
items.content: Diluting vodka with water reduces the overall alcohol concentration, which may lower the risk of rapid intoxication.

items.title: Improved hydration
items.content: The water component helps maintain the body’s fluid balance when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Fewer calories
items.content: Dilution decreases the calorie count per serving compared with straight vodka.

items.title: Alcohol effects
items.content: Despite dilution, the product still contains alcohol and can cause intoxication if over‑consumed.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol may amplify the effects of certain medicines, so caution is advised.

items.title: Not suitable for pregnancy
items.content: Any alcohol consumption is contraindicated for pregnant women.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the vodka‑water blend chilled, optionally over ice with a slice of lemon or lime. It works well as a base for light cocktails such as a Vodka Tonic, Cosmopolitan, or simple Vodka Soda.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, it is best used within 3–6 months to preserve flavor and aroma.
